title: One Word Beginnings
author: Kurt Wootton
summary: This article describes the design of a One Word opening activity for Habla's 18th Annual Teacher Institute, built around the theme of the role of analog experiences in the classroom. Drawing on Robert Macfarlane's book The Lost Words—written after the Oxford Junior Dictionary omitted dozens of nature words in favor of technology terms—the activity asks participants to identify one word they never want to lose, a word holding personal, cultural, or emotional significance. The resulting sequence moves from individual reflection to small-group sharing, then to a full-room Sound and Movement circle where each participant speaks their word aloud synchronized to a full-body movement, with the whole room echoing back. The article uses this opening design to model a broader pedagogical principle: that learning environments must begin by welcoming participants personally, sharing a clear roadmap, and creating an immediate experience of community before content begins. The accompanying reflection on writing style—that grammar mistakes and typos reveal humanness, and that deliberately rougher writing may be worth preserving as AI smooths everything else—connects the activity's theme to a broader question about analog experience in a digital world.
points: The One Word opening activity inverts the problem of lost words: instead of mourning what has been removed from the dictionary, participants identify words they personally refuse to lose—words from family, work, culture, or memory.

Robert Macfarlane's Lost Words was written after the 2007 Oxford Junior Dictionary omitted words like blackberry, almond, chestnut, and cauliflower while adding paste, broadband, and ironically analogue—reflecting children's declining connection to the natural world.

The Sound and Movement circle—where each participant says their word aloud synchronized with a full-body movement while the whole room echoes—creates an almost immediate sense of collective belonging, especially among strangers.

The activity models a three-part opening structure applicable to any learning environment: a welcoming space with personal greetings, a clear roadmap of what is coming, and an immediate community-building experience.

The author's reflection on AI smoothing writing errors raises the question of whether deliberately preserving roughness—grammar mistakes, typos, personal quirks—is a way of keeping the human voice visible in an AI-saturated world.
quotes: The 2007 and 2012 editions omitted the words blackberry, almond, cauliflower, and chestnut and added the words paste, broadband, and ironically analogue to give just a few examples.

There is a shocking, proven connection between the decline in natural play and the decline in children’s wellbeing. Compared with a generation ago, when 40% of children regularly played in natural areas, now only 10% do so, while another 40% never play anywhere outdoors.

Grammar mistakes and typos reveal that we are human, that we miss things. In the last book I wrote with my co-author Eileen Landay, we didn’t have AI and I’m still catching mistakes the many eyes on it missed.

Entering a new space with strangers can always be difficult, and anxiety-provoking for some. When I have a new group of people in the room I always like to let them know where we are heading— what each day will look like, who will be presenting, what time we are eating lunch, and what the end product of our work might look like.
I’ve found that this echoing by the whole group creates a feeling that we are all in this together—it almost immediately offers a shared sense of community.
Last summer we looked at the implications of AI in learning which, after a week of conversations and workshops, led us to the question, 'What makes us human?'
